title: Domain and fraction-field transfer through unit denominators
statement:
Let $A$ be a commutative integral domain, $B$ a commutative ring, and $i:A	o B$ an injective unital ring homomorphism. Assume that for every $x\in B$ there are $a,s\in A$ such that $i(s)$ is a unit of $B$ and $i(s)x=i(a)$. Then $B$ is an integral domain. Writing $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ and $\operatorname{Frac}(B)$ for their fields of fractions, there exists a ring isomorphism $J:\operatorname{Frac}(A)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{Frac}(B)$ satisfying $J(a/s)=i(a)/i(s)$ for all $a,s\in A$ with $s
e0$. In particular $J$ extends $i$. For $x,y\in B$ with $y
e0$, and $a,s,b,t\in A$ with $i(s),i(t)$ units, $i(s)x=i(a)$ and $i(t)y=i(b)$, one has $s b
e0$ and $J((t a)/(s b))=x/y$. Here an integral domain means a nonzero commutative ring without zero divisors; a unit is an element with a multiplicative inverse. For a domain $D$, $\operatorname{Frac}(D)$ is the field [def-weil-field] of pairs $a/s$ with $s
e0$, modulo $a/s=a^{\prime}/s^{\prime}$ if and only if $as^{\prime}=a^{\prime}s$, with the usual fraction sum and product.

proof.text: For $xy=0$ in $B$, choose $i(s)x=i(a)$ and $i(t)y=i(b)$ with $i(s),i(t)$ units. Then $i(ab)=i(s)i(t)xy=0=i(0)$, so injectivity gives $ab=0$. Since $A$ is a domain, $a=0$ or $b=0$. Multiplication by the inverse of $i(s)$ or $i(t)$ gives $x=0$ or $y=0$, respectively. Together with step 1 this proves that $B$ is an integral domain.

proof.text: Use the fraction model in the statement and the nonzero-inverse property of [def-weil-field]. Write $k:B\to\operatorname{Frac}(B)$ for $z\mapsto z/1$; the fraction equality criterion makes $k$ injective. For $s\ne0$, injectivity gives $i(s)\ne0$. Define $J(a/s)=k(i(a))/k(i(s))$. If $a/s=c/u$, then $au=cs$; applying $k\circ i$ proves equality of the proposed images by cross multiplication. Thus $J$ is well defined. The fraction formulas give $J((au+cs)/(su))=J(a/s)+J(c/u)$ and $J(ac/(su))=J(a/s)J(c/u)$. Also $J(0/1)=0$ and $J(1/1)=1$. Hence $J$ is a unital ring map and $J(a/1)=k(i(a))$.
